questions.stem: Consider this: A nephew promising to pay an uncle asks whether a promise is enforceable. The promise was made after the work was done. Which statement best states the governing legal rule on these facts?

options.text: Only payment of money can count as consideration on these facts.
A promise is supported by consideration whenever the promisor had a good reason to make it on these facts.
Consideration requires a bargained-for exchange in which each party gives or promises something of legal value in return for the other's promise on these facts.
A promise made as a gift is enforceable because it is still a promise on these facts.

questions.explanation: Consideration is what distinguishes a bargain from a gift. The promise and the return must be linked as part of an exchange, so a benefit that was not sought in return for the promise does not qualify. Here the decisive point is bargained-for exchange, so the result follows from that doctrine rather than from the surface appeal of a competing statement. Each distractor rests on a different mistake about how the doctrine operates.
questions.hint: Ask what each party gave in exchange for the other's promise. Keep the inquiry on bargained-for exchange.
